theme: Pusan crisis, land reform, POW command chain
findings: 1949 land reform attribution is multi-institutional: Assembly passage, presidential veto, Assembly override, presidential promulgation, later implementation expenditure.
A 1950 Embassy report shows land reform implementation had moved forward by spring 1950, so the December 1949 implementation-delay snapshot must not be treated as the final outcome.
In the 1952 Pusan crisis, the explicit proposal to arrest all Assemblymen is attributed by a contemporaneous diplomatic report to Home Minister Yi Pom-suk, not President Rhee.

Rhee's June 25 letter asserted a Communist conspiracy as justification, while a June 2 US policy memorandum states US/UN authorities did not believe the evidence supported that claim. Preserve as conflict pending Korean prosecution files.

On June 18 1953 Rhee explicitly self-attributed the POW release order and said he deliberately withheld the plan in advance; this strongly verifies top-level authorship but not camp-level operational authorship.
leadQueue: National Assembly stenographic record: reconstruct April-June 1949 land reform bill, veto and override vote.
ROK Gazette: obtain the June 1949 promulgated land reform text and presidential countersignature chain.
Cabinet minutes: identify the June 1949 reasons for Rhee's land reform veto.
Finance records: verify the 100 billion won implementation expenditure authorized by Rhee in late 1949.
Agriculture Ministry records: identify implementation directives before the 1950 spring planting season.
UN A/1881 p49: compare English land reform law text with Korean promulgated text.
1950 tenant-transfer registers: test Embassy claim that tenant farmers were already becoming owner-operators.
Rhee Oct 23 1950 statement: locate Korean OPI original on extending land policy northward.
1952 martial-law proclamation: obtain Korean original, legal basis, signatories and countersignatures.
May 24 1952 appointment records: verify Yi Pom-suk, Hong Pom-hui and Yun-kyong titles in Korean sources.
So Min-ho arrest file: obtain warrant, charges, interrogation and disposition.
Other arrested legislators: identify names, warrants, arresting units and release dates.
Cabinet minutes around June 4 1952: verify Yi Pom-suk arrest-all proposal in Korean provenance.
Prime Minister records: reconstruct the compromise constitutional amendment drafted during the crisis.
National Assembly record July 1952: verify vote attendance, police presence and exact amendment tally.
UNCURK A/2187: extract its account of coercion and compare with FRUS editorial notes.
ROK prosecution files: test Rhee's claimed Communist conspiracy against actual charges and evidence.
Police command records: map Yi Pom-suk to national police personnel and operational directives.
Military police orders: separate martial-law enforcement from individual Assembly arrest decisions.
Van Fleet telegram 1178 May 28 1952: recover full text on army opposition to political use.
Telegram 1160 May 26 1952: recover full Embassy account behind FRUS d138.
Telegram 1244 June 2 1952: recover full record of Rhee's reported 24-hour dissolution ultimatum.
June 18 1953 Korean presidential statement: locate Korean-language OPI S-61 original.
Military police camp orders June 18 1953: identify transmission time and issuing officers.
Provincial governor circulars June 18-19 1953: trace reception and care instructions for released POWs.
Defense Ministry chain June 18 1953: establish Shin Tae-yong's knowledge and implementation role.
Prime Minister Paek Tu-chin records: establish when he first learned of the POW release plan.
Foreign Minister Pyun Yong-tae letter to Clark June 18 1953: compare diplomatic justification with Rhee's statement.
Camp-by-camp release logs: distinguish presidential decision from local operational methods and casualties.
JCS/ROK military records 1953-54: trace how POW release changed US contingency planning and Korean command relations.
